steps.claim: The ten most-streamed albums drop, from Drake's Scorpion to Taylor Swift's Midnights

test.source: “Smartphones, Online Music Streaming, and Traffic Fatalities,” JAMA Network Open, 2026

steps.note: The study takes the ten albums with the most first-day streams from 2017 to 2022. Dated here to the first of those release days, Scorpion on June 29, 2018.

steps.claim: Big release days saw about 18 more deaths on US roads

test.design: release days against the 10 days before and after
test.source: “Smartphones, Online Music Streaming, and Traffic Fatalities,” JAMA Network Open, 2026
test.effect: 18.2 more US traffic deaths on an average release day, a 15.1% rise, as streaming jumped 43%

event.key: change in US road deaths each day, with its 95% range (the paper’s Figure 2A)

fx.unit: people killed on US roads that day
fx.quote: The adjusted number of US traffic fatalities was 139.1 (95% CI, 126.8-151.4) on album release days compared with 120.9 (95% CI, 119.6-122.2) on the 10 days before and after the release
fx.say: more deaths on US roads on release day, as streaming rose 43%
fx.ci_quote: an absolute increase of 18.2 fatalities (95% CI, 4.8-31.7 fatalities; P = .01)

test.why: Drivers probably stream the new album on their phones while driving, which distracts them.
test.why_quote: suggesting that online music streaming through smartphones may significantly contribute to distracted driving and traffic fatalities

steps.note: From the paper: “major music album releases, accompanied by increased online streaming, were associated with a significant increase in traffic fatalities.” The extra deaths were higher among younger male drivers, crashes with one person in the car and cars with built-in infotainment screens. The paper’s averages are 120.9 deaths on a usual day and 139.1 on a release day, 18.2 extra; its 95% range for the extra runs from 4.8 to 31.7.

steps.claim: A European football club with an African player loses a close game

test.source: “Do Politically Irrelevant Events Cause Conflict? The Cross-continental Effects of European Professional Football on Protests in Africa,” International Organization, 2023

steps.note: The study covers 15,102 close games from 2005 to 2019. Dated here to the first year.

steps.claim: More peaceful protests in the player's home country after his club loses a close game

test.design: close losses against draws, adjusted for the betting odds
test.source: “Do Politically Irrelevant Events Cause Conflict? The Cross-continental Effects of European Professional Football on Protests in Africa,” International Organization, 2023
test.effect: more peaceful protests in the player's home country after a close loss, with no change in riots or armed conflict
test.why: A close loss makes people trust their country's leader less, and that lost trust leads to protests.
test.why_quote: Close losses also temporarily decrease people's trust in their country's leader.

steps.note: From the paper: “close losses of African players’ teams increase peaceful protests in their original countries while not changing the likelihood of riots or armed conflicts.” An earlier version (IDE Discussion Paper 866, 2022) put the rise at nearly double the usual protest rate. Close wins did not lower protests.

steps.claim: A truck attack on a Stockholm shopping street kills five people

test.source: “The effect of a terrorist attack on emergency department inflow: an observation study using difference-in-differences methodology,” Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine, 2019

steps.note: The attack came on April 7, 2017, the Friday a week before Good Friday.

steps.claim: Fewer people went to Stockholm's emergency rooms for about three weeks

test.design: difference in differences against the same hospitals in 2013 to 2016
test.source: “The effect of a terrorist attack on emergency department inflow: an observation study using difference-in-differences methodology,” Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine, 2019
test.effect: 7% to 9% fewer emergency room visits, strongest near the attack and back to normal in about three weeks
test.why: After the attack, some patients probably chose to wait or stay away from the emergency room.
test.why_quote: the results suggest that some patients actively choose when, where and if they should go to the ED

fx.unit: emergency room visits after the attack, against earlier years

steps.note: From the paper: “The study shows a statistically significant reduction in overall ED inflow of 7-9% following the attack.” The drop faded with distance and was not significant beyond 10 km. ED means an emergency department.

steps.claim: Greece moves its clocks forward an hour each spring

test.source: “Summertime and the drivin’ is easy? Daylight saving time and vehicle accidents,” Health Economics, 2023

steps.note: The study covers every spring and fall clock change from 2006 to 2016. Dated here to the first year.

steps.claim: Fewer serious road crashes in the days after the clocks go forward

test.design: regression discontinuity at the clock change
test.source: “Summertime and the drivin’ is easy? Daylight saving time and vehicle accidents,” Health Economics, 2023
test.effect: 15% to 20% fewer serious crashes after the spring change, strongest in the hours the change affects most
test.why: Moving the clocks changes how much light there is on the road, and more light makes serious crashes less likely.
test.why_quote: support an ambient light mechanism that reduces the counts of serious vehicle accidents during the Spring transition

fx.unit: serious road crashes after the spring clock change
fx.quote: 15% to 20% fewer serious crashes after the spring change

steps.note: From the paper: “The sizable discontinuity parameters suggest that the Spring transition causes a 15%–20% decrease in serious crashes.” Minor crashes rose about 13% after the fall change. Quoted from the published article's open copy at City, University of London.

steps.claim: Britain moves its clocks forward in spring and back in fall

test.source: “Road traffic casualties in Great Britain at daylight savings time transitions: a causal regression discontinuity design analysis,” BMJ Open, 2022

steps.note: The study covers both clock changes in every year from 2005 to 2018. Dated here to the first year.

steps.claim: Slightly fewer road casualties right after the clocks change

test.design: regression discontinuity at the clock changes
test.source: “Road traffic casualties in Great Britain at daylight savings time transitions: a causal regression discontinuity design analysis,” BMJ Open, 2022
test.effect: about 4.7 fewer road casualties and 0.75 fewer deaths a year across both changes, a minor drop

fx.unit: change in road casualties and deaths a year, both clock changes
fx.quote: about 4.7 fewer road casualties and 0.75 fewer deaths a year across both changes

steps.note: From the paper: “All significant average treatment effects are negative (54 significant models out of 287 estimated), indicating that there are fewer casualties following the transitions.” The authors say this does not support a UK parliamentary estimate of 30 fewer deaths a year if the clock changes ended.

steps.claim: Terror attacks in Barcelona and Cambrils kill sixteen people

test.source: “Terrorist attacks, Islamophobia and newborns’ health,” Journal of Health Economics, 2021

steps.note: The first attack came in Barcelona on the afternoon of August 17, 2017.

steps.claim: More low-birth-weight babies born to mothers from Muslim countries in the towns attacked

test.design: triple difference by the mother's origin, her town, and before or after
test.source: “Terrorist attacks, Islamophobia and newborns’ health,” Journal of Health Economics, 2021
test.effect: the share of low-birth-weight babies rose 23.77% and deliveries with complications 13.02% among mothers from Muslim countries in Barcelona, Cambrils and Ripoll
test.why: Stress from rising Islamophobia after the attacks probably hurt the health of babies at birth.
test.why_quote: We conclude that Islamophobia-related stress is possibly one of the channels affecting health at birth.

fx.unit: births to mothers from Muslim countries, against what was expected
fx.quote: the share of low-birth-weight babies rose 23.77% and deliveries with complications 13.02%

steps.note: From the paper: “Results show that the share of low-birth-weight babies and deliveries with complications raise significantly by 23.77%, and 13.02%.” The study counts only babies conceived before the attacks. It also found more Islamophobia and more emotional distress in the same group.

steps.claim: Undersea fiber cables bring broadband internet to Senegal

test.source: “Impact of Broadband Internet on Preventive Healthcare Behaviors in Senegal,” Economie et Statistique / Economics and Statistics, 2024

steps.note: The cables arrived in 2010. Dated here to that year.

steps.claim: More young children slept under a bednet in homes near the new fiber line

test.design: difference in differences, homes near the fiber line against homes farther away
test.source: “Impact of Broadband Internet on Preventive Healthcare Behaviors in Senegal,” Economie et Statistique / Economics and Statistics, 2024
test.effect: 7.8 to 14.3 percentage points more homes where children under 5 slept under a bednet the night before
test.why: Broadband let people read health information online, and that probably changed their health habits.
test.why_quote: The arrival of optic fiber submarine cables in 2010 brought broadband connectivity to Senegal, allowing access to healthcare information online.

fx.unit: percentage points more homes with a child under 5 under a bednet, out of 100
fx.quote: 7.8 to 14.3 percentage points more homes where children under 5 slept under a bednet the night before

steps.note: From the paper: “Broadband access is found to be positively associated with the use of bednet.” The 7.8-point estimate matches mothers on place, wealth, education and more; the 14.3-point one uses fixed effects. Results for prenatal care were mixed, and child vaccination did not change.

steps.claim: The iPhone goes on sale in the US, only through AT&T

test.source: “Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly,” NBER Working Paper 35310, 2026

steps.note: AT&T kept the iPhone to itself until February 2011. The study uses that: it compares counties by how much of them AT&T’s 3G network reached.

steps.claim: Fewer babies born to teenagers where AT&T’s network reached

test.design: counties by AT&T 3G coverage, synthetic difference-in-differences and Poisson event studies
test.source: “Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly,” NBER Working Paper 35310, 2026
test.effect: 4.5% to 8.0% fewer births at ages 15 to 19 where the iPhone could be used. Nationally the teen birth rate fell from 41.5 to 31.2 per 1,000 from 2007 to 2011; without the iPhone the paper puts 2011 at 33.4 to 34.4, so the iPhone accounts for 21% to 31% of the drop

lines.key: teen births per 1,000 women: what happened, and the paper’s estimate without the iPhone (shaded; Figure 6)

test.why: People with an iPhone probably spent less time face to face, used more pornography, and had sex less often.
test.why_quote: National-survey evidence on time use and sexual behavior is consistent with the iPhone reducing in-person interactions, increasing pornography use, and reducing sexual frequency.

steps.note: From the paper: “access to the iPhone reduced births by 4.5–8.0% at ages 15–19 and 3.2–6.6% at ages 20–24.” Running the same test on Verizon’s and Sprint’s networks finds nothing. A working paper: not yet peer reviewed. The chart’s 2007 and 2011 values are from the paper’s text; 2008 to 2010 are read off its Figure 6, the low edge of the band from the Poisson estimate and the high edge from the synthetic difference-in-differences one. Quoted from the NBER abstract and the authors’ open copy.

title: Mass shootings before an election (2016 and 2020)

steps.claim: A mass shooting happens near home in the six months before a presidential election

test.source: “The effect of mass shootings on voter turnout in the United States,” Science Advances, 2025

steps.note: The study covers the 2016 and 2020 elections. Dated here to 2016.

steps.claim: Turnout rose in the blocks nearest the shooting

test.design: regression discontinuity in time: shootings just before the election against shootings just after
test.source: “The effect of mass shootings on voter turnout in the United States,” Science Advances, 2025
test.effect: almost 10 points higher turnout in the blocks nearest the shooting and 3 to 4 points a little farther out, with no change in how people voted for president
test.why: A shooting nearby probably makes gun violence stand out as a local issue, so people nearby are more likely to vote.
test.why_quote: Our results show the (geographically bounded) salience of mass shootings for local political engagement and ballot reform efforts.

fx.unit: points of turnout added (the paper says almost 10 for the nearest blocks)
fx.quote: almost 10 points higher turnout in the blocks nearest the shooting and 3 to 4 points a little farther out

steps.note: From the paper: “we find that mass shootings mobilize local voters (especially in heavily Democratic areas) but do not shift presidential vote choices.” The study uses turnout for every census block group in the 2016 and 2020 elections and the Gun Violence Archive's public mass shootings within six months of each. The whole rise came in neighborhoods where Clinton or Biden won 80% or more of the vote.

title: Mass shootings and alcohol sales (2006 to 2019)

steps.claim: A mass shooting happens in the community

test.source: “Mass shootings durably increase the sale of alcohol in American communities,” PNAS Nexus, 2024

steps.note: The study covers 326 mass shootings from 2006 to 2019. Dated here to the first year.

steps.claim: Stores in the area sold more alcohol for at least two years

test.design: difference in differences with fixed-effects counterfactuals, by three-digit ZIP area and week
test.source: “Mass shootings durably increase the sale of alcohol in American communities,” PNAS Nexus, 2024
test.effect: about $22,000 more alcohol sold a week across the area for two years, a 3.5% rise, and 5.5% after shootings in public places; no rise after shootings in homes
test.why: Shootings leave a community with trauma, and people probably cope by changing their habits, including buying more alcohol.
test.why_quote: Communities can cope with the ensuing trauma in a number of ways, including changing their behavioral patterns.

fx.unit: weekly alcohol sales in the area, against what was expected
fx.quote: a 3.5% rise, and 5.5% after shootings in public places

steps.note: From the paper: “a mass shooting in a given community (the area covered by the ZIP-3 code) predicts a significant increase in the sales of alcohol that lasts at least 2 years past the shooting.” The data are weekly sales at 35,000 stores. Across all shootings the rise just clears the usual test (p = 0.048); after public shootings it is larger.

steps.claim: Chile switches to daylight saving time each year

test.source: “Daylight Saving Time and Automobile Accidents: Evidence From Chile,” Health Economics, 2025

steps.note: The study covers every clock change in Chile from 2002 to 2018. Dated here to the first year.

steps.claim: Fewer car accidents while daylight saving time is on

test.design: regression discontinuity at the clock change, plus difference in differences on the shifting start dates
test.source: “Daylight Saving Time and Automobile Accidents: Evidence From Chile,” Health Economics, 2025
test.effect: 2.7% fewer car accidents under daylight saving time, though 6% more in the first week after the clocks go forward
test.why: Daylight saving shifts when it is light out, and more light on the road means fewer serious and fatal crashes.
test.why_quote: also find evidence that ambient light reduces serious and fatal accident risk

fx.quote: 2.7% fewer car accidents under daylight saving time, though 6% more in the first week after the clocks go forward

steps.note: From the paper: “I find a 2.7% reduction in automobile accidents under the DST regime.” The first week after the clocks go forward saw 6% more accidents, which the author ties, as suggestive evidence, to lost sleep.
